analysis.investment_thesis: A 2022-incorporated EV two-wheeler maker with a 54 Cr market cap and a 0.47% ROE is precisely the sort of unproven, capital-intensive, no-moat business I would never own. The trailing P/E of 8x is a statistical illusion — on that return on equity, the business is destroying value, not compounding it.
key_strengths: Promoter skin-in-the-game at 69.31% aligns ownership interest
Small reported P/E of 8.21 suggests nominal earnings exist
Operating in a growing EV category with policy tailwinds
key_risks: ROE of 0.47% — the business barely earns anything on its equity
Incorporated 2022: zero long-term track record, no demonstrable moat
Indian EV 2W/3W space is brutally competitive (Ola, TVS, Bajaj, Ather) with heavy capex
red_flags: Sub-1% ROE is a fundamental capital-allocation failure
No institutional (DII 0%) validation of the story
Micro-cap EV manufacturer — classic speculative IPO-era profile outside my circle of competence
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Charlie and I have a simple rule: we want businesses that earn high returns on the capital employed in them, run by honest people, at sensible prices. Supertech EV fails the first and most important test decisively — a 0.47% ROE means shareholders would earn more in a savings account with none of the risk. A low headline P/E of 8 is meaningless when the "E" is a rounding error on the equity base; this is not cheapness, it is a warning sign that earnings are negligible relative to capital deployed.

The business itself — a four-year-old EV scooter and e-rickshaw assembler competing against deep-pocketed giants like Bajaj, TVS, Ola, and Ather — has no evident moat, no brand equity, no cost advantage, and no switching costs. The industry is capital-intensive, technologically shifting, and price-competitive — the exact combination we spent 60 years avoiding. High promoter holding is a modest positive, but it cannot offset the absence of durable economics. I would put this squarely in the "too hard" pile and move on.
